<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 8476, the No Antisemitism in Education Act of 2026, would require local education agencies (LEAs) and institutions of higher education (IHEs) that receive federal financial assistance, as a condition of receiving such assistance, to ``treat discrimination that is motivated by antisemitism . . . as vigorously as such agency or institution treats all other forms of discrimination prohibited by title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.''\1\ The bill further requires the federal government, LEAs and IHEs to use the definition of antisemitism developed by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) and its working examples when determining whether relevant federal law has been violated.\2\ H.R. 8476 would place an unworkable and likely unconstitutional standard in federal law. It would also call into question a longstanding interpretation of civil rights law in a way that might result in fewer students having civil rights protections.
\1\H.R. 8476 Sec. 3 119th Cong. (2026).
\2\Id.
H.R. 8476 UPSETS LONGSTANDING INTERPRETATION OF RELIGION AND TITLE VI
FOR ONLY ONE RELIGION
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VI) states in part, ``No person in the United States shall, on the ground of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.''\3\ Religion is not a class protected from discrimination under the text of Title VI.\4\ However, since at least the early 2000s, there has been a recognition at the Department of Education (ED or Department) Office for Civil Rights (OCR), that there are instances of religious discrimination that, when analyzed are the result of discrimination based on shared ancestry and national origin.\5\ As such, what might appear to be religious discrimination, unactionable under Title VI, is instead discrimination based on national origin or shared ancestry, illegal under Title VI.\6\ This interpretation has held over both Republican and Democratic administrations.\7\ H.R. 8476 seems to turn this longstanding interpretation on its head.
\3\42 U.S.C. Sec. 2000d.
\4\Other titles of the law specifically include religion. See 42 U.S.C. Sec. 2000e-2(a) (``It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer--(1) to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin;'') (emphasis added).
\5\Dear Colleague Letter from The Hon. Kenneth Marcus, Deputy Assistant Sec'y for C.R., Off. for C.R., U.S. Dep't of Educ. (September 13, 2004), https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ocr/ religious-rights2004.html (``Groups that face discrimination on the basis of shared ethnic characteristics may not be denied the protection of our civil rights laws on the ground that they also share a common faith. Similarly, the existence of facts indicative of religious discrimination does not divest OCR of jurisdiction to investigate and remedy allegations of race or ethnic discrimination. OCR will exercise its jurisdiction to enforce the Title VI prohibition against national origin discrimination, regardless of whether the groups targeted for discrimination also exhibit religious characteristics.'').
\6\Id.
\7\E.g., Letter from The Hon. Thomas Perez, Asst. Atty. Gen., U.S. Dep't of Justice, to The Hon. Russlyn Ali, Asst. Secy. for C.R., U.S. Dep't of Educ. (Sept. 8, 2010) (``Although Title VI does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of religion, discrimination against Jews, Muslims, Sikhs, and members of other religious groups violates Title VI when that discrimination is based on the group's actual or perceived shared ancestry or ethnic characteristics, rather than its members' religious practice . . . The inquiry into whether a particular act of alleged discrimination falls within the purview of Title VI's prohibitions will, in every case, involve a detailed analysis of the allegations to determine whether jurisdiction is appropriate.'').
H.R. 8476 attempts to make all antisemitic discrimination actionable under Title VI, without amending Title VI. Specifically, the bill directs recipients of federal financial assistance to treat antisemitic discrimination the same as discrimination that is actionable under Title VI.\8\ The bill proposes to use the same enforcement provisions as Title VI.\9\ The bill's findings section decries an alleged ``double standard'' between antisemitic incidents generally, and incidents that are actionable under Title VI.\10\ In sum, the aim of H.R. 8476 is to elevate all antisemitic discrimination (actions rotted in anti-Jewish animus) to be actionable under Title VI.
\8\H.R. 8476 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
\9\Id.
\10\H.R. 8476 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 8476 is problematic for multiple reasons. First, the bill would be applicable to only one form of religious discrimination--that against the Jewish faith--in a statute (Title VI of the Civil Act) that currently does not expressly identify religion as a protected class. While the bill's findings section complains of a double standard, H.R. 8476 would literally create a unique standard only to address anti- Jewish animus and no other forms of religious animus. This is problematic since the federal government has long recognized other religions, like Judaism, face a heightened chance of Title VI discrimination on the basis of shared ancestry or national origin (Islam, Sikhism, Buddhism). By not including these religions, the implication is that these forms of discrimination are somehow not as deserving of the same treatment as antisemitic discrimination. Further the definition of antisemitism in the bill would make activity far beyond shared identity or national origin discrimination actionable, but only for antisemitism. For example, a Sikh or Muslim student would only be protected if the discrimination they experienced could be traced to their shared identity or national origin; whereas a Jewish student would have a definition would provide protection well beyond the confines of national origin or shared identity discrimination. On its face, H.R. 8476 bestows preferential review of discrimination of Jewish students and not the religion animus directed at others.
H.R. 8476'S DEFINITION OF ``ANTISEMITISM'' IS UNNECESSARY, LIKELY
UNCONSTITUTIONAL
The problem with H.R. 8476's definition of ``antisemitism'' does not stop there. The bill incorporates via cross-reference the definition of antisemitism developed by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).\11\ The use of this definition has been a hotly debated topic since before the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. The IHRA definition (and its working examples) equate certain manifestations of anti-Zionism and criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and free speech advocates worry it can be used to chill speech that would not, in most cases be considered antisemitic.\12\ Keneth Stern, the lead drafter of the IHRA definition, testified in the Senate that he does not think it should be used in educational settings.\13\
\11\H.R. 8476 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026); Exec. Order No. 13899
Sec. 2, 84 Fed. Reg. 68,779 (Dec. 11, 2019).
\12\E.g., Letter to The Hon. Miguel Cardona, Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Educ. from Christopher Anders & Jenna Levantoff, Am. C.L. Union (Feb. 6, 2024), https://www.aclu.org/documents/ reject-definitions-of-anti-semitism-that-encompass-protected-speech.
\13\Antisemitic Disruptions on Campus: Ensuring Safe Learning Environments for All Students, Hearing before the S. Comm. on Health, Educ. Lab. & Pensions, 119th Cong. (2025), https://www.help.senate.gov/ imo/media/doc/06e69363-9e5d-54f9-8019-dbe95168b2a9/Stern%20 Testimony.pdf; Kenneth Stern, A Bad Deal: By Adopting the IHRA Definition of Antisemitism, Universities are Sacrificing Academic Freedom, Knight First Amendment Inst. at Columbia U., Sept. 5, 2025, https://knightcolumbia.org/content/a-bad-deal-why-using-the-ihra-definition-of-antisemitism-on-campus-is-incompatible-with-academic-freedom-and-students-right-to-open-inquiry.
Since Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attack on Israel and the subsequent protests in many American educational systems, there have been many cases brought against IHEs claiming that they allowed hostile learning environments to exist on campus. Namely, there have been increase allegations of antisemitic in education settings.\14\ These cases often turn on whether public statements made by students or faculty protesting the ongoing war in Gaza can be considered harassment under Title VI. In one of these cases, Stand with Us v. MIT, the First Circuit Court of Appeals found that

at the Israeli state and its treatment of

in its legal sidebar on the Stand with Us v. MIT case noting
The contemporary examples identified by the IHRA
include types of speech close to those that Stand With
Us determined are not inherently antisemitic. Examples
include ``[d]enying the Jewish people their right to
self-determination, e.g., by claiming that the
existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor,''
``[a]pplying double standards by requiring of [Israel]
a behavior not expected or demanded of any other
democratic nation,'' and ``[d]rawing comparisons of
contemporary Israeli policy to that of the Nazis.'' In
general, courts determine the boundaries of protected
speech, and Congress cannot remove speech from the

reasoning of Stand With Us could find that the
definition of antisemitism promoted by the IHRA sweeps
in First Amendment-protected speech, which would
restrict Congress's ability to regulate it.\16\

Aside from the Constitutional considerations, the definition of antisemitism from H.R. 8476 is not necessary. Title VI does not provide definitions of discrimination on the basis of race, color or national origin. There is not some set of magic words that evince racial discriminatory intent. Further, the protected class in question, Jewish students, is not defined by the definition of antisemitism present in the bill. The pertinent legal question is whether a Jewish student was treated differently as a result of being a member of a protected class. It is unclear how the proposed definition provides relevant information to answer that question. As the recently updated Title VI Legal Manual from the Department of
Justice states:

ultimately employed, the central question remains
whether the recipient acted intentionally based on
race, color, or national origin. In evaluating the
totality of relevant facts, courts and federal funding
